chapters.title: Chapter 4: Cost Advantages, Scale, and Distribution

lessons.title: Location and Resource Advantages: Cement, Mining, and Utilities

body.text: Some advantages cannot be built, bought, or copied, only owned: the limestone next to the plant, the ore body with the richest grade, the pipeline already laid under the city.

children.text: The last lesson covered cost advantages that companies create through process and scale. This lesson covers advantages that come from where a company is and what it controls. They are among the hardest moats for a rival to replicate, because no amount of money creates a second deposit in the same place. But they also come with an important limit: they usually sit inside commodity or regulated industries, where the moat protects the company's cost position far more than its selling price.
Three Kinds of Place-Based Advantage

body.caption: Location, resource, and infrastructure advantages in India

cells: Heavy, low-value products are expensive to transport, so the nearest plant to a market wins on delivered cost
Cement makers such as UltraTech and Shree Cement, whose regional plants serve markets within a limited distance
Ownership of rich, low-cost natural deposits keeps production cost below most global rivals
Hindustan Zinc's high-grade zinc mines; NMDC's iron ore mines; Coal India's large open-cast coal mines
A pipeline or grid, once built, is uneconomic to duplicate, making the owner a natural monopoly in its area
Indraprastha Gas and Mahanagar Gas city gas networks; Power Grid Corporation's transmission network

children.text: Location: Why Cement Is a Regional Business

markDefs.definition: The maximum distance a product can be transported to customers while still being competitive on delivered price. For cement in India, typically a few hundred kilometres by road.

children.text: A bag of cement is heavy and cheap relative to its weight. Moving it far quickly eats the profit, so each plant has an effective
economic radius
beyond which it cannot compete with a closer plant. India's cement industry is really a set of regional markets, not one national market.
Worked Example: Two Plants, One Market

Both plants produce cement at ₹4,000 per tonne and sell into the same city at ₹6,000 per tonne (about ₹300 per 50 kg bag). Road freight costs roughly ₹2.5 per tonne per kilometre. Plant A is 150 km from the city. Plant B is 600 km away.

Plant A earns more than three times Plant B's margin on every tonne, with identical factories. If prices fall by ₹600 a tonne in a slowdown, Plant A still makes ₹1,025 while Plant B loses ₹100 on every tonne it ships. A well-located plant sets the floor that distant rivals cannot survive below.

body.title: Price the Distance
body.prompt: A cement company is considering supplying a market 400 km further away than its current customers. If freight costs ₹2.5 per tonne per kilometre, how much extra freight cost does each tonne carry?
body.explanation: Extra freight = 400 km × ₹2.5 = ₹1,000 per tonne. On a selling price of around ₹6,000 per tonne, that is roughly a sixth of revenue, often enough to wipe out most of the margin.

body.text: Location protects a cement plant from distant competitors, not from new capacity next door. When several companies expand in the same region at once, local prices fall and even well-located plants see returns shrink. That is why cement ROCE across the industry tends to swing with regional capacity additions, and why many cement companies struggle to earn returns well above their cost of capital across a full cycle.

children.text: Resources: Owning the Low End of the Cost Curve

markDefs.definition: A chart ranking all producers of a commodity from lowest to highest cost of production. The market price tends to settle around the cost of the highest-cost producer still needed to meet demand.

children.text: In commodities such as zinc, iron ore, and coal, every producer sells a near-identical product at a market price. The advantage goes to the company with the lowest cost of production. Analysts visualise this with a
cost curve

body.title: Illustrative Cost Curve: Cash Cost per Tonne ($) vs Market Price

children.text: At a market price of $125, Producer A earns $45 a tonne and Producer E loses $25. If the price drops to $100 in a downturn, Producer A still earns $20, Producer B earns $5, and Producers C, D, and E are all losing money and may cut output. The low-cost producer survives every downturn and profits in every upturn. Hindustan Zinc, with its high-grade Rajasthan mines, has long been described as sitting in the lowest-cost part of the global zinc cost curve.

body.title: Why the highest-cost producer sets the price

children.text: Demand for a commodity has to be met by someone. If demand is high enough that even the most expensive mines are needed, the price must rise enough to cover their costs, or they would shut and supply would fall short.

Every lower-cost producer sells at that same market price, so the difference between their cost and the price is pure margin. When demand falls and the most expensive producers are no longer needed, the price settles lower, closer to the cost of the next producer up the curve.
A resource moat is therefore a position on this curve. The company does not control the price, but it controls how much of the price it keeps.
Coal India: Scale Plus Resource

body.title: India's coal production by producer, FY24 (approximate share %)

children.text: Coal India produces roughly three-quarters of India's coal, largely from big open-cast mines that are cheaper to operate than underground mining. That combination of resource quality and scale is a real cost advantage. But the government is both its majority owner and a strong influence on coal pricing, and commercial coal mining was opened to private companies in 2020. The resource is durable; how much of its value reaches minority shareholders is decided partly by policy.
Infrastructure: Natural Monopolies and Regulated Returns

markDefs.definition: A market where one supplier can serve all customers at lower cost than two or more competitors could, usually because of very high fixed infrastructure costs.

children.text: Some infrastructure is simply uneconomic to build twice. No city needs two networks of gas pipelines under its roads, or two parallel high-voltage transmission lines on the same route. The owner becomes a
natural monopoly
. Because monopolies can overcharge, regulators usually control their returns.

body.title: Resource moat vs regulated infrastructure moat

columns.label: Resource moat (e.g. mining)
points: Profits swing with global commodity prices
The company keeps the upside in a boom
Downturns hurt, but low-cost producers survive
Returns can be very high at cycle peaks
Key risk: prolonged low prices and policy intervention

columns.label: Regulated infrastructure moat (e.g. transmission, city gas)
points: Upside is capped by the regulator's allowed return
Demand is steady and competition is limited
Returns are reasonable but rarely spectacular
Key risk: changes to regulated returns or technology shifts

children.text: Power Grid Corporation earns a return on equity set by the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) on its transmission assets, a figure in the mid-teens. City gas distributors such as Indraprastha Gas in Delhi and Mahanagar Gas in Mumbai own pipeline networks authorised by the Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board (PNGRB). Their moats are real, but they face a different kind of threat: the shift of vehicles from CNG to electric could shrink a large part of their demand even though no rival can build a competing pipeline.

body.label: The place-based moat question
body.value: Does the advantage protect the price the company charges, or only its cost?
body.context: Location and resource moats mostly protect cost position in industries where the price is set by the market. Judge them by returns across a full cycle, not at the peak.

body.title: Which Advantage Is Most Durable?
body.question: Which of these is the most durable place-based advantage?
options: A cement plant in a region where three competitors are adding large new capacity next year
A mine with one of the world's highest-grade deposits of a metal, with decades of reserves
A power plant that sells electricity at spot prices with no long-term contracts
A logistics company whose main warehouse is close to a highway
body.explanation: A high-grade deposit with long reserve life keeps a producer low on the cost curve for decades, and no rival can replicate the deposit. The cement plant faces new local capacity. The spot power plant has no protected position. A warehouse near a highway is easily matched by another warehouse.

body.title: Complete the Principle
body.textWithBlank: In a commodity industry, the market price tends to be set by the cost of the highest-cost producer still needed to meet demand, so a low-cost producer earns the difference as ___.
body.explanation: Low-cost producers sell at the same market price as everyone else. Their lower cost becomes margin, and it protects them when prices fall.

body.title: The City Gas Dilemma
body.scenario: You are researching a listed city gas distribution company that holds the pipeline network in a large Indian metro. It has earned ROCE above 20% for years, has almost no debt, and faces no competing pipeline. About half its gas volumes go to CNG vehicles, mainly autos, taxis, and buses. The state government has announced incentives to shift public transport and commercial vehicles to electric over the next decade.
body.prompt: Is this company's moat widening, stable, or at risk? What would you monitor?
body.modelAnswer: The infrastructure moat itself is intact: no rival will build a second pipeline network, and the company still controls gas supply to homes, industry, and commercial users. But a moat protects against competitors, not against demand disappearing. With about half of volumes from CNG vehicles, a large shift to electric public and commercial transport could shrink the most important part of the business, even without any competitor. So the moat is stable but the territory it protects may shrink. What to monitor: CNG volume growth each quarter versus residential, industrial, and commercial volumes; the pace of electric bus and commercial vehicle adoption in its city; whether the company is diversifying into new geographic areas, industrial customers, or EV charging; margins per unit of gas, which show whether it can pass through gas cost changes; and any changes in PNGRB rules on network access. The valuation should reflect a business whose largest segment faces structural decline, not one with unlimited growth.

body.text: Companies named are used to illustrate concepts from public information and are not investment recommendations. Coal production shares are approximate and for illustration. Cement, cost curve, and city gas examples use hypothetical figures; check current regulatory and company disclosures before relying on any detail.

points: Location, resource, and infrastructure advantages come from what a company owns and where it operates, and money cannot create a second one in the same place
Cement is regional because freight costs limit how far a plant can compete, so well-located plants earn higher margins at the same price
Location does not protect against new capacity next door, which is why cement returns swing with regional supply
In commodities, low-cost producers keep the gap between market price and their cost, surviving downturns that force high-cost rivals out
Infrastructure natural monopolies like city gas networks and transmission grids are durable but usually have regulated or capped returns
Place-based moats mostly protect cost, not price, so judge them on returns across a full cycle and watch for policy and technology shifts
